name: Zebu cattle domestication in the Indus Valley
summary: Evidence points to northwestern South Asia as a centre of zebu domestication, with the earliest date still disputed.
description: Bone measurements at Mehrgarh document changes in cattle size across the Neolithic sequence. A 2023 cattle-genome study cited earlier archaeological work to place domesticated indicine cattle in the Indus Valley about 8000 years ago. New dates for Mehrgarh’s human cemetery challenge the chronology underlying that early estimate. The genome study also reports later dispersal of zebu across parts of Asia and into Africa.

impact.note: The source reports zebu spreading from the Indus Valley across South Asia and into south-west, central and east Asia and Africa, so many societies on two continents; a large herd animal was a new capability for these farmers, and the heat-tolerant breeds and crosses are its direct successors.

date.label: Proposed c. 6050 BCE (chronology disputed)
date.basis: Chen et al. cite archaeology for approximately 8000 years before present. Mutin et al. subsequently proposed a later chronology for the aceramic cemetery at Mehrgarh.

events.statement: A genome study, citing archaeological evidence, places domesticated indicine cattle in the Indus Valley at about 8000 years before present (c. 6050 BCE, counting from 1950).

evidence.supports: Archaeological evidence indicates the presence of domesticated indicine cattle earlier in the Indus Valley (~8000 YBP) than in South India (~5000 YBP) and the middle Ganges (~4000 YBP)

evidence.locator: pp. 90–94, Figs. 7.1–7.2 and text on Bos
evidence.supports: Primary bone measurements show changing cattle size distributions across the archaeological sequence at Mehrgarh.
The new model dates the start of the human cemetery to 5200–4900 BCE and challenges the earlier site chronology used to contextualize cattle remains.

events.caveats: The approximately 6050 BCE estimate comes from the archaeology cited by Chen et al. New dates for the cemetery concern human enamel. Direct dating of taxonomically diagnostic cattle remains remains necessary to settle the earliest evidence.

date.label: about 5000 years before present (c. 3050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Indicine cattle began to spread from the Indus Valley about 5000 years before present (c. 3050 BCE, counting from 1950), later reaching south-west and central Asia, east Asia and Africa.

evidence.supports: The global dispersal of indicine cattle started in the Indus Valley at ~5000 YBP, followed by their spread into Southwest and Central Asia, East Asia, and Africa between 4000 and 1300 YBP

earliest_record.rationale: The reported early date is disputed. The later dispersal estimate does not resolve the earliest archaeological occurrence in the Indus Valley.

unresolved.note: The Indus Valley coordinates are a rough regional centre, not a site.

Directly date taxonomically diagnostic bovine specimens and match them to the faunal sequence. Secure sampled dates and ancient genomes could clarify whether cattle management at Mehrgarh drew on earlier western farming practices.

evidence.locator: pp. 90–94, Figs. 7.1–7.2 and text on Bos
evidence.supports: Primary bone measurements show changing cattle size distributions across the archaeological sequence at Mehrgarh.
The new model dates the start of the human cemetery to 5200–4900 BCE and challenges the earlier site chronology used to contextualize cattle remains.

research.note: The earlier chronology is retained as an attributed historical estimate. The earliest date of domestication is unresolved.

caveats: The regional domestication chronology remains open. The human cemetery dates at Mehrgarh do not directly date the cattle bones.
